question: How have open-source publishing platforms impacted the global distribution of academic publishing?
answer:
The global distribution of academic publishing has historically been characterized by a significant geographical imbalance, with the majority of international journals possessing wide reach located in Western countries, resulting in limited distribution to the Global South . This structural disparity means that the broader ecosystem of academic publishing remains fairly unbalanced, as most international journals are concentrated in Western nations . In response to the challenges posed by this centralized model and the difficulty in accessing information regarding e-publishing tools and services, which is often hard to obtain or tends not to be passed on, the CARPET platform was developed to provide information on e-publishing technology and support the sustainability of e-publishing projects .

The emergence of open-source publishing platforms has fundamentally altered the dynamics of content distribution by enabling a shift away from exclusive publisher control. The Open Journal Systems (OJS) platform, for instance, was enabled by the combined ethos of the Open Source software movement, which also facilitated the development of the Open Access approach as an exemplar for moving academic publishing forward and opening up routes to publication . With the rise of open access, academic social networks, and piracy websites, publishers are no longer in total control over how academics access published content . This loss of control has been further exacerbated by the fact that open access articles now appear in a wide range of locations, including faculty websites, institutional and subject repositories, and academic social networks, thereby legally circumventing publisher control .

To address the struggle within the academic community to regain the capacity to act on the extent of public circulation of their work, the creation of open source scholarly publishing platforms has become a central strategy . These platforms facilitate the proliferation of open access publications across the web through the use of Creative Commons licenses, which allow for permission-free sharing without publisher mediation . Furthermore, the integration of peer review boards within these open frameworks has assisted in raising the quality of submissions from developing countries, helping them approach international standards . While the consulted records did not surface specific quantitative metrics regarding the extent of this geographical redistribution, the qualitative evidence indicates a move toward a more decentralized and accessible global publishing infrastructure driven by open-source technologies and open access principles.

question: How has the citation graph been used to improve neural language models for scientific papers?
answer:
The integration of citation graph structures into neural language models for scientific papers has evolved from enhancing information extraction and summarization to supporting advanced retrieval-augmented generation for large language models. A foundational approach, CitationIE, explores the use of citation graph information in neural scientific information extraction by leveraging either the graph structure or the content of citing and cited documents . The paper states that combining this citation graph information with document text leads to strong improvements in salient entity classification and relation extraction . This integration increases the end-to-end performance of the information extraction system over strong baselines . The underlying rationale for this approach is that in a citation graph, adjacent paper nodes share related scientific terms and topics .

In the domain of summarization, the citation graph is utilized to convey unique structural information regarding document-level relatedness, which is applicable to summarization tasks . The paper states that the citation graph can assist in generating high-quality summaries . This is supported by the observation that reference papers within a research community are very similar in content, logic, and writing style to the source paper . To leverage this, MUS (Multi-granularity Unsupervised Summarization) was proposed as a simple, low-cost solution for extractive summarization .

More recently, the application of citation graphs has extended to Large Language Models (LLMs) through retrieval-augmented generation. SciRAG is described as an adaptive, citation-aware, and outline-guided system for retrieval and synthesis of scientific literature . This system addresses the challenge of whether papers use different Question and Answer (Q&A) formats to clarify intent and compose more complicated prompts to LLMs . The use of Q&A formats to clarify user intent and enhance prompt composition is noted as gaining prominence . These developments occur in the context of LLMs, which are AI systems whose primary knowledge consists of statistical patterns, semantic relationships, and syntactical structures , and which are adept at complex tasks despite having limited forms of knowledge .

Regarding specific architectural mechanisms, quantitative performance metrics, and the genealogical evolution of these approaches, the consulted records did not surface detailed information. Specifically, there are no recorded configurations, main results, or lineage outputs for the "citation graph" entity , and no lineage edges or genealogy are recorded for this concept . Consequently, the exact architectural details of how CitationIE, MUS, or SciRAG implement citation graph integration, as well as specific numerical improvements, are not present in the available data.

question: How have theories of distributed cognition informed the design of features in social computing systems?
answer:
The knowledge base contains a meaningful but limited set of papers that trace the arc from distributed cognition theory to social computing design. Below is a synthesis of what the corpus surfaces, with honest disclosure of where the evidence is thin.

**Theoretical foundation: distributed cognition as a design framework**

The foundational 2000 paper by Hutchins (and colleagues) explicitly proposes distributed cognition "as a new foundation for human-computer interaction," arguing it "provides a radical reorientation of how to think about designing and supporting human-computer interaction" [sciverse_distributed_cognition]. The theory is "specifically tailored to understanding interactions among people and technologies" [sciverse_distributed_cognition], identifying "cognitive agents, processes, events within an environment and beyond the 'skin or skull of an individual'" [sciverse_a_tale_of_two_perspectives]. A later paper restates that distributed cognition theory "provides an effective theoretical foundation for understanding human-computer interaction and a fertile framework for designing and evaluating digital" systems, citing Hollan et al. [sciverse_a_tale_of_two_perspectives]. The aircraft cockpit case study in that same paper illustrates the design implication: what matters is not individual pilot skill but the environmental and systemic factors that support the crew's collective cognitive performance [sciverse_a_tale_of_two_perspectives].

**Application to group and social dynamics**

The 2009 paper "Group Intelligence: A Distributed Cognition Perspective" explicitly frames group intelligence through the distributed cognition lens, noting that "theories of social psychology and cognitive science provide diverse and enlightening perspectives of group dynamics, adaptive behavior, networks of social relationships" [sciverse_group_intelligence_a_distributed_cognition_perspective]. The paper builds a model that "visualizes different theoretical aspects of the theory of distributed cognition" as applied to group-level cognition [sciverse_group_intelligence_a_distributed_cognition_perspective]. This is the most direct bridge in the corpus between distributed cognition theory and social/group computing contexts.

**Design patterns and artifact ecologies**

A paper on "artifact ecologies as shared spaces" reports having "examined different design patterns for distributed cognition in a controlled experiment among software practitioners" [sciverse_from_behaviour_to_design_implications_for_artifact_ecologies_as_shared_spaces_fo]. This suggests that distributed cognition has been operationalized into concrete design patterns for collaborative software environments, though the specific patterns are not detailed in the records my search surfaced.

**Compatibility with user-facing feature design**

A paper on "challenging the phenomena of technology" draws a direct design implication: "Distributed Cognition is compatible with different users encountering different features of the same experience" [sciverse_challenging_the_phenomena_of_technology]. This is a key design principle for social computing: the same system can present different feature subsets to different users while maintaining a coherent shared cognitive space.

**Social media feed customization (2025)**

The most recent and most directly social-computing-relevant paper in the corpus is "Designing Usable Controls for Customizable Social Media Feeds" (2025) [sciverse_designing_usable_controls_for_customizable_social_media_feeds]. It identifies "a natural tradeoff between the expressiveness of a system and its understandability" [sciverse_designing_usable_controls_for_customizable_social_media_feeds] and applies the Interactive Machine Teaching (IMT) framework to feed customization [sciverse_designing_usable_controls_for_customizable_social_media_feeds]. While this paper addresses the design of user-facing controls in a social computing system, my search did not surface an explicit citation of distributed cognition theory within it; the connection to distributed cognition is inferential (the tradeoff between expressiveness and understandability, and the design of shared yet customizable interfaces, are themes consistent with distributed cognition's emphasis on the system-environment as the unit of analysis).

**What my search did not surface**

- I did not find a paper in the corpus that explicitly names "social computing" as its domain AND explicitly cites distributed cognition as its theoretical framework in the same record. The bridge is built across multiple papers: the foundational theory [sciverse_distributed_cognition], the group-intelligence application [sciverse_group_intelligence_a_distributed_cognition_perspective], the design-patterns experiment [sciverse_from_behaviour_to_design_implications_for_artifact_ecologies_as_shared_spaces_fo], and the social media feed design [sciverse_designing_usable_controls_for_customizable_social_media_feeds].
- I did not find specific feature-level design decisions (e.g., "we added a shared annotation panel because distributed cognition suggests X") attributed to distributed cognition in a social computing system. The corpus records are at the level of theoretical framing and design principles rather than granular feature specifications.
- Lineage queries for "distributed cognition" with relation "informs" did not return explicit edges to social computing design papers, suggesting the corpus does not encode a direct citation lineage between the foundational distributed cognition papers and the social computing design papers.

**Summary of the design principles that have been drawn from distributed cognition for social computing systems, as evidenced in this corpus:**

1. **The system-environment is the unit of analysis**, not the individual user — design should focus on how artifacts, representations, and coordination mechanisms in the shared environment support collective cognition [sciverse_distributed_cognition, sciverse_a_tale_of_two_perspectives].
2. **Different users can encounter different features of the same experience** while the system maintains a coherent shared cognitive space [sciverse_challenging_the_phenomena_of_technology].
3. **Group-level intelligence emerges from the interaction of individuals with shared artifacts and representations**, not from summing individual capabilities [sciverse_group_intelligence_a_distributed_cognition_perspective].
4. **Design patterns for distributed cognition** can be experimentally evaluated in collaborative software settings [sciverse_from_behaviour_to_design_implications_for_artifact_ecologies_as_shared_spaces_fo].
5. **There is a tradeoff between expressiveness and understandability** in user-facing controls, which must be managed when designing customizable social media features [sciverse_designing_usable_controls_for_customizable_social_media_feeds].

question: How has literature discussed AI as a design material?
answer:
The literature characterizes Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a design material primarily within the Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) community, where it has recently been highlighted as a distinct resource for design . This conceptualization is described as a call for interaction designers to consider intelligence itself as a resource, rather than merely a tool or component . Consequently, the view of intelligence as a design material necessitates a deeper understanding of how intelligence functions in this capacity . HCI researchers and designers have investigated this idea to explore AI's potential in improving interactions with applications and software systems .

A significant portion of the literature focuses on the challenges and complexities inherent in working with AI as a material. Researchers have investigated the specific challenges for UX practitioners, noting the complexity of the material itself . These challenges include a lack of clear understanding of AI's capabilities, difficulties in envisioning uses that do not yet exist, and other obstacles . Furthermore, designers, who are often novices in machine learning, experience difficulties and bottlenecks while working with AI . The materiality of AI is further complicated by the fragility, incompleteness, and opacity of models such as topic models, where even minor changes can induce large and potentially undesirable changes in the resulting model . In the context of user interactions, these interactions often negatively affect the quality of the resulting modelling in ways that can be difficult for the user to evaluate .

The literature also discusses the integration of AI into existing design workflows and tools. New AI generation tools, such as Midjourney and Stable Diffusion, have been incorporated into participants' daily routines . These AI tools are used alongside creative design platforms such as Figma, Adobe XD, and Adobe Illustrator . Additionally, general purpose conversational AI platforms, including ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, Perplexity, and Gemini, are characterized by their chat-based interfaces where users type prompts or upload documents to receive text responses .

While the notes provide specific insights into the challenges and tools associated with AI as a design material, the consulted records did not surface detailed discussions regarding the specific arguments of the "User Ex Machina" paper beyond the noted impacts on modelling quality, nor did they provide detailed accounts of the "from behaviour to design" paper's specific contributions to the materiality of AI, aside from its examination of distributed cognition design patterns in software teams   . Similarly, the records did not surface detailed information on the "from pen to prompt" paper's specific discussion of AI as material in writing practice, nor did they provide detailed elaborations on the "towards human-ai synergy in ui design" paper's broader theoretical stance on AI as material beyond the mention of tool integration, nor did they offer detailed insights into the "wikipedia ores explorer" paper beyond the mention of designer difficulties    .

question: How is artificial intelligence being utilized to enhance the diagnosis and treatment of sleep apnea?
answer:
Artificial intelligence is increasingly utilized to address the significant public health burden of sleep apnea, a condition described as a chronic and highly prevalent disease that remains underdiagnosed and untreated in a substantial number of adult patients [coarse:2e20f53dadc1] [coarse:25a826ec71fc]. While the gold standard for diagnosis remains in-laboratory nocturnal polysomnography (PSG) [coarse:445fc17b8e28], the widespread implementation of machine learning technologies for big data analysis and prediction tools offers a relevant step forward in the intricate scenario of sleep apnea diagnosis and phenotypization [coarse:4953ee5bf04a] [coarse:1411614e7f94]. The most important applications of artificial intelligence in obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) have been identified as predicting treatment outcomes, improving treatment options, and personalizing treatment [coarse:e3d2367b08b6].

In the domain of diagnosis, AI methods are being applied to overcome the limitations of traditional visual scoring, which suffers from subjectivity and inter-rater variability when identifying sleep stages in overnight PSG data that utilizes EEG as a sensing modality [arxiv_2012.06104#63450]. Specific machine learning approaches cited in the literature include the use of Recurrent Deep Neural Networks for real-time sleep stage classification from single-channel EEG, as restated from the work of Bresch et al. (2018) [arxiv_2012.06104#129600]. Additionally, a state space and density estimation framework for sleep staging in obstructive sleep apnea has been proposed, as restated from the work of Kang et al. (2018) [arxiv_2012.06104#130950]. Further diagnostic automation involves the automated identification of sleep disorder types using triplet half-band filters and ensemble machine learning techniques with EEG signals, as restated from the work of Sharma et al. (2021) [arxiv_2403.17561#326700]. Beyond EEG-based PSG, 24-hour ECG analysis has been utilized to determine the sleep apnea index (AI) in patients with heart rhythm disorders; in this pilot study, patients with an AI greater than 5 were referred for further diagnostic evaluation of sleep apnea [coarse:d4cf84106741] [coarse:d856d632530a].

Regarding treatment, if sleep apnea is confirmed in a specialized laboratory, Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) is considered the best form of treatment, with patients also advised to correct living habits and reduce or eliminate the use of medications predisposing to respiratory distress, such as sedatives [coarse:917a4cfc8217] [coarse:475c5c735bab]. The consulted records did not surface specific details regarding AI methods used for CPAP adherence or the specific performance metrics and results reported for the diagnostic and treatment algorithms mentioned.
